list.listitem: Cyanide can cause rapidly fatal poisoning following exposure by the oral, inhalation, and dermal routes. Only acute cyanide poisoning is considered in this chapter.
Acute cyanide poisoning can be rapidly fatal following ingestion, inhalation, or dermal exposure.
The most common cause of acute cyanide poisoning is inhalation of fire smoke in enclosed spaces. B

Four specific cyanide antidotes are available in various countries throughout the world, and all are efficacious. However, hydroxocobalamin is considered safe, based on reported use and adverse effects in the largest number of patients, allowing empirical prehospital and hospital administration in cases of suspected cyanide poisoning, including smoke inhalation victims. B
Hydroxocobalamin may be associated with increased acute kidney injury (AKI) in patients requiring intensive care unit (ICU) treatment and with methemoglobinemia.

Approximately 4000 deaths from smoke inhalation occur in the United States each year, and cyanide is implicated in 33% to 90% of these deaths. Cyanide was detected in blood from 59% of fire-related fatalities and 50% of fire survivors in one study.

Cyanide ingestion is another source of cyanide poisoning. In a 7-year retrospective case series conducted in 61 US poison centers, almost half (45%) of the 435 ingestions (of 1741 cyanide exposures) were intentional, most commonly a suicide attempt. Most patients were male (68%) with a mean age of 34 years (range 1 month to 83 years). While relatively few patients died (8.3%), 9% (38/435) of patients had cardiac arrest or hypotension and relatively few (13% of all cases) received an antidote.

In another case series of 213 non-pharmaceutical exposure suicides in San Diego County, inhaled toxins were most often used (81%) most often carbon monoxide. Ethylene glycol and cyanide (8 cases or 3.7%) were used in a relatively constant manner over the 12 years of study.

In a retrospective case series from the UK of calls to the National Poisons Information Service between 2008 and 2019, 1252 cases of suspected cyanide poisoning were identified of whom 239 (19%) involved children under age 10 years.

An outbreak of cyanide poisoning from contaminated Cassava flour was reported in Uganda in 2017. There were 98 probable cases and 2 deaths. Associated signs and symptoms were vomiting (95%), diarrhea (87%), malaise (60%), dizziness (48%), tachypnea (27%), syncope (16%), and tachycardia (10%) and fever (6%).
Fourteen cases with 2 fatalities were reported from the Philippines in 2015 linked to intake of insufficiently prepared bitter cassava.

The major source of cyanide exposure in the United States is from enclosed-space fire smoke inhalation. In addition to particulates, irritants, and carbon monoxide, fire smoke can contain significant amounts of cyanide.

In the UK case series, noted above, the most common exposures were ingestion of plant material (35%) and smoke inhalation (32%),`` with smoke inhalation causing the majority of severe and fatal cases (139; 71%).

Data from France and Australia indicate that one of the major determinants of survival is the blood cyanide level. In aircraft crashes, fatalities not due to trauma are usually due to smoke inhalation.
Burning or smoldering natural (eg, wood, wool, silk) and synthetic plastic (eg, polyacrylonitrile, polyurethane) products can release cyanide during pyrolysis.

Information on cyanide as an industrial contaminant and as a potential bioterrorism agent can be found on the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention website under the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health and Emergency Preparedness. There are also several papers discussing hazardous chemical emergencies and attempts to identify an antidote that is safe, effective, easy to administer, and has a rapid onset of action.
Based on data from the Global Terrorism Database 1970-2019, of the 292 terrorist attacks involving a chemical agent as a primary attack method recorded, cyanide was used in 21 (7.2%).

Some cyanide and cyanogenic compounds are:
Acetonitrile (cyanogenic compound; delayed poisoning) Acrylonitrile (cyanogenic compound; delayed poisoning; also hepatoxicity from the parent compound) Hydrogen cyanide (gas) Hydrocyanic acid (liquid) Calcium cyanide (salt; solid) Cyanogen halides (gases/liquids; cyanogen bromide; cyanogen chloride; cyanogen iodide) Laetrile (solid; bogus cancer drug) Vitamin B17 (tablets; bogus cancer drug) Plants of the Rosaceae that contain amygdalin, most notably apricot seeds, but also present in peach, plum, loquat, apple and bayberry. Amygdalin's toxicity is caused by its decomposite product of benzaldehyde and hydrogen cyanide after primarily oral ingestion. To limit toxicity, oral doses ranging from 0.6 g to 1 g per day or IV administration can be used. Data do not support use of amygdalin as a dietary supplement for cancer treatment. "Bitter" (cyanide-rich) cassava (paralytic disease called konzo) Although cyanide poisoning has a role in the development of konzo, malnutrition also appears to be a risk factor; cases of konzo occur without either condition. Foods commonly available among the Korean population that contain cyanogenic glycosides are Cassava chips (lotaustralin), apple seeds (prunasin and dhurrin), and Prunus mume axis (taxiphyllin). High-dose nitroprusside (IV drug for cardiac afterload reduction and blood pressure control) Potassium cyanide (salt; solid; used in jewelry or textile industries) Sodium cyanide (salt; solid)

Cyanide binds to and inhibits cytochrome a-a3 oxidase in the mitochondrial electron transport chain, preventing utilization of oxygen in oxidative phosphorylation. This severely decreases adenosine triphosphate production, forces cells to switch to anaerobic metabolism, and generates lactic acid.

The organs most affected are those with the greatest oxygen demand, the myocardium and brain. This results in the three hypoxias of cyanide poisoning: (1) histotoxic hypoxia from inhibition of cytochrome oxidase, (2) hypoxic hypoxia from depression of the central respiratory drive, and (3) stagnation hypoxia from depression of myocardial contractility.
The onset of severe signs and symptoms is quite rapid following inhalation or dermal exposure. With ingestion exposure, the onset of severe signs and symptoms may be delayed for 30 to 60 minutes.

Following inhalation, the half-life (t-½) of cyanide in blood is approximately 0.5 to 1 hour. This is also the t-½ following ingestion in the acute phase once the peak blood level has been reached. The terminal phase (when blood levels are below the generally recognized toxic limit) is approximately 19.5 hours.
Following ingestion, other toxicokinetic parameters are: area under the curve: 48 mcg-hours/mL; volume of distribution: 0.41 L/kg for humans; and clearance: 1.63 L/min.
Ingestion: 200 to 300 mg of cyanide salts or 50 mg of hydrocyanic acid may be fatal in adults.
Inhalation: Inhalation exposure to 200 to 300 mg/m3 (180-270 ppm) may be rapidly fatal.
Early/mild cyanide poisoning signs and symptoms may mimic anxiety attacks or hyperventilation syndrome: giddiness, headache, anxiety, tachycardia, hyperpnea, mild hypertension, and palpitations.

Later/more severe acute cyanide poisoning signs and symptoms can include: nausea and vomiting, tachycardia or bradycardia, hypotension, seizures or coma, apnea, and mydriasis (usually sluggishly reactive to light).

Other signs of more severe poisoning include cardiac dysrhythmias and blocks, asystole, ischemic ECG changes, cardiovascular shock, noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, respiratory failure, lactic acidosis, and ultimately death.

In a review of 102 patients with isolated cyanide poisoning, most patients were unresponsive (78%), hypotensive (54%, with 39% requiring vasopressor support), or had respiratory failure (73%), and most (66%) required intubation with mechanical ventilation. Cardiac arrest or seizures occurred in 20%. Less common were cyanosis (15%), cherry red skin (11%), and odor present (15%).

In the UK case series, 40 patients (3%) died. Clinical features associated with death were cardiac arrest (OR 36.4, 95% CI 14.4-92.2), hypotension (OR 15.8, 7.0-35.9), coma (OR 10.8, 5.6-21.0) and lactic acidosis (OR 7.8, 4.1-14.8).

The European expert consensus document suggests that cyanide toxicity be suspected with the following: (a) a history of enclosed-space fire; (b) any alteration in the level of consciousness; (c) any cardiovascular changes (particularly inexplicable hypotension); and (d) elevated plasma lactate.

Whole blood cyanide levels take, at best, several hours to obtain and cannot be used to make decisions about emergent treatment. Cyanide concentrations of 0.5 to 1 mg/L are considered mild, between 1 and 2 mg/L are moderate, between 2 and 3 mg/L are severe and greater than 3 mg/L is considered lethal. The following laboratory tests can be used to support a clinical impression of possible cyanide poisoning: Plasma lactate: best correlated with the presence of a significant cyanide poisoning. Levels of more than 8 mmol/L in pure cyanide poisoning and more than 10 mmol/L in smoke inhalation victims can be very suggestive of cyanide poisoning. In the UK case series, a serum lactate <2.0 mmol/L was associated with Poisoning Severity Score None or Minor (sensitivity 76%; specificity 86%) and >11 mmol/L was associated with fatality (sensitivity 74%; specificity 80%). However, in one case report, a lower level of serum lactate correlated with a higher level of serum cyanide that could benefit from treatment. Plasma lactate level does not appear to be altered by venous vs. arterial origin of blood samples but may be falsely elevated by a delay of 2 hours between blood draw and sample measurement or if obtained shortly after completion of hydroxocobalamin administration. Arterial blood gases: metabolic acidosis (sometimes severe), relatively normal O2 saturation and pO2 (if the patient is breathing spontaneously or being ventilated). Anion gap: elevated anion gap is indicative of acidosis and suggests cyanide poisoning. Venous pO2 or O2 saturation: an elevated venous pO2 or O2 saturation indicates that the body is unable to extract oxygen from the blood. This occurs in any cytochrome oxidase poisoning (cyanide, hydrogen sulfide, sodium azide) but also in septic shock. Its presence suggests cyanide poisoning, but its absence does not rule out cyanide poisoning. Whole blood cyanide levels cannot be obtained rapidly enough to guide emergent treatment, but should be obtained in all suspected cases to confirm the diagnosis. Techniques are under development for rapid detection of blood cyanide.
Hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α) is under investigation as an early predictor of acute hydrogen cyanamide poisoning.

ABCs: Ensure airway patency with any means up to and including endotracheal intubation; ensure that the patient is breathing adequately or provide assisted ventilation as required; patients with known or suspected cyanide poisoning and all smoke inhalation victims should be given 100% oxygen; insert at least one large-bore IV line.
Advanced lifesaving (ALS) medications: None of the standard ALS medications are contraindicated in patients with cyanide poisoning.
Anticonvulsants: Seizures are not common in cyanide poisoning, but if they do occur, administer standard anticonvulsant medications.

Decontamination: Patients with dermal exposure should have contaminated clothing removed and be decontaminated with copious amounts of water or suitable alternative decontamination solutions. Patients exposed by inhalation should be removed from the toxic atmosphere by rescuers wearing appropriate personal protective equipment. Further decontamination is generally unnecessary. Patients ingesting cyanide compounds should be given activated charcoal. Syrup of ipecac is contraindicated in cyanide poisoning and gastric aspiration is of questionable value, except perhaps in cases of ingestion of liquid cyanogenic compounds such as acetonitrile if the patient presents to the hospital within 1 hour of ingestion.

Treatment algorithms: Developed by the European consensus conference, patients are divided into three groups based on the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) (https://www.cdc.gov/masstrauma/resources/gcs.pdf) and vital signs.

Prehospital treatment: After administration of 100% oxygen, those with no neurologic or hemodynamic compromise and a GCS >14 are monitored while those with intermediate (GCS 10-13 and/or abnormal vital signs) or severe (GCS <9) poisoning are given 5 g of hydroxocobalamin at 70 mg/kg or up to 10 g if in cardiac arrest. Blood samples are drawn for cyanide testing if possible

Hospital treatment: Following a history, physical exam, and laboratory tests (lactates, blood carboxyhemoglobin [HbCO], arterial and venous blood gas, electrocardiogram, and other tests as needed), victims with significant trauma or burns are triaged, those with evidence of carbon monoxide are treated (HbCO >10%), and the remainder are treated based on suspicion and serum lactate. If lactate is high, patients are treated with 5 g of hydroxocobalamin (70 mg/kg) and lactate is rechecked in 2 hours. If the level remains high, patients who were pretreated in route to the hospital with hydroxocobalamin are considered for sodium thiosulphate and admitted for end-organ monitoring and those not pretreated are given a second dose of 5 g of hydroxocobalamin. If the latter have a high lactate at 2 hours, they are considered for sodium thiosulphate and monitoring.

Authors of a study evaluating time to administration of hydroxocobalamin and clinical characteristics in an academic medical center found a significant delay with a median time to hydroxocobalamin administration of 208 minutes (IQR 62.5 to 330). Hydroxocobalamin was given within 60 minutes of arrival in 12 cases, 3 of whom died. Time to hydroxocobalamin administration was longer in death cases than for survivors (median 221 minutes [IQR 119 to 594] and median 184.5 minutes [IQR 62.8 to 315], respectively).
Elimination half-life of compounds like acetonitrile that metabolize to cyanide may extend to more than 24 hours necessitating continued antidote administration.

The Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry also offers guidance for medical management of cyanide poisoning. They recommend use of either the standard cyanide antidotal kit that includes amyl nitrite perles and intravenous infusions of sodium nitrite and sodium thiosulfate or the cyanokit that employs intravenous infusion of hydroxocobalamin (see below).

Drugs under investigation : Beta-agonists, pulmonary blood flow modifiers, anticoagulants and antiinflammatory agents. Sulfanegen, based on 3-mercaptopyruvate sulfurtransferase, is under testing as another intramuscular antidote. Carnosic acid and nitrocobinamide have been tested in animals and look promising. Cellular-based therapies such as antioxidants and succinate prodrugs to provide metabolic support for cells.

Other treatments : In a report of self-induced poisoning using sodium ferrocyanide and methanol in a patient who presented with unconsciousness, acute kidney injury and severe metabolic acidosis, use of gastric lavage, bicarbonate, ethanol, plasmapheresis and continuous renal replacement therapy were successful in achieving full recovery.

There are four specific cyanide antidotes in clinical use worldwide: amyl nitrite/sodium nitrite/sodium thiosulfate (Lilly Kit, Pasadena Kit, Taylor Kit; used in the United States): 4-dimethylaminophenol (4-DMAP) (Germany); dicobalt-EDTA (Kelocyanor; used in the United Kingdom, Australia, and France); and hydroxocobalamin (Cyanokit; used in France and the United States). These work through a variety of mechanisms including chelation; formation of stable, less toxic complexes; methemoglobin induction; and sulfane sulfur supplementation for detoxification by endogenous rhodanese.

There have been no comparative or placebo-controlled trials of antidotes. In a systematic review of case series, hydroxocobalamin was used in 361 cases with many survivors and no serious adverse effects reported. Sodium thiosulphate use was reported in two case series with no adverse effects. A combination of sodium nitrite, amyl nitrite and sodium thiosulphate was used in 74 patients with similar results reported. Only single case reports of dicobalt edetate or 4-dimethylaminophenol were found. Hydroxocobalamin and sodium thiosulphate appear to have the fewest adverse effects.
Variations of the Taylor Kit have been being used in the US since the 1930s. The kit contains the following components:

Amyl nitrite: As pearls to be broken and administered by inhalation, either placed in gauze and held near the nose and mouth of spontaneously breathing patients or placed inside the resuscitation bag or into the lip of the face mask in ventilated patients. Use a new pearl every 1 to 2 minutes until an IV line is secured, and then discontinue and administer IV sodium nitrite. Amyl nitrite is relatively contraindicated in enclosed-space fire smoke inhalation victims. Amyl nitrite pearls placed into the lip of a face mask and used with an oxygen-powered breathing device have been used successfully to resuscitate workers with industrial airborne hydrogen cyanide exposure.

S odium nitrite: Sodium nitrite is supplied in 10-mL vials for IV injection in the Taylor Kit. The adult dose is 10 mL of a 3% solution given IV over absolutely no less than 5 minutes. The pediatric dose is 0.12 to 0.33 mL/kg also given over absolutely no less than 5 minutes. A second dose, one-half the first dose, may be given 30 minutes later if there is inadequate clinical response. Adverse effects: hypotension when administered too rapidly. This can compromise severely cyanide-poisoned patients, who are usually already hypotensive. Methemoglobin induction has led to fatal methemoglobinemia in children mistakenly administered adult doses. Methemoglobin induction can also further decrease oxygen-carrying capacity in smoke inhalation victims with combined carbon monoxide and cyanide poisoning. Sodium nitrite is relatively contraindicated in smoke inhalation victims.

Sodium thiosulfate: Sodium thiosulfate is a sulfur donor. The availability of sulfane sulfur is the rate-limiting step for cyanide detoxification to much less toxic thiocyanate by the endogenous enzyme rhodanese. The adult dose is 12.5 g, administered IV following sodium nitrite. The pediatric dose is 1.65 mL/kg. Sodium thiosulfate is generally thought to act too slowly to be used as the only antidote in pure cyanide or smoke inhalation cases. Adverse effects: in normal volunteers, injection site reactions, nausea, and retching/vomiting have been reported.

4-Dimethylphenol (4-DMAP) is a methemoglobin inducer but lacks the hypotensive effects of the nitrites in the Taylor kit. Potential adverse effects include: excessive methemoglobin induction with resultant decreased oxygen transport capability, intravascular hemolysis, and liver and kidney toxicity. It is an efficacious cyanide antidote but is relatively contraindicated in smoke inhalation victims. The usual adult dose is 250 mg administered IV. Pediatric doses have not been established.

Dicobalt-EDTA is a cobalt-containing direct cyanide chelating antidote. Cyanide and cobalt are mutually antidotal. When dicobalt-EDTA is administered in the absence of cyanide, manifestations of severe cobalt toxicity can occur, such as severe hypertension followed by hypotension, chest pain, cardiac dysrhythmias, and cardiovascular collapse. Other adverse effects include: vomiting, facial edema with potential upper airway compromise, urticaria, anaphylactic shock, and seizures.

In general, dicobalt-EDTA is recommended for administration only to patients with clearly established cyanide poisoning. It is relatively contraindicated in smoke inhalation victims. The usual adult dose is 300 mg to 600 mg IV, each 300 mg dose followed by IV administration of 25 mL to 50 mL of 50% dextrose. Pediatric doses have not been established.

Hydroxocobalamin (Cyanokit) has been used for a number of years in France and was approved by the US FDA in December 2006. It is especially useful in the prehospital setting due to its safety and ease of administration.

Adult dose: 2 vials of 2.5 g each (5 g total dose), each vial of lyophilized hydroxocobalamin reconstituted in 100 mL of normal saline and given intramuscularly. D5W or Ringer's lactate may be used if normal saline is not available. May repeat once (total dose 10 g) if the clinical response is inadequate.
Pediatric dose: No pediatric dose has been established. However, a dose of 70 mg/kg has been suggested based on limited pediatric experience and extrapolation from animal studies and adult doses.

Adverse effects: nearly all patients have transient reddish brown discoloration of the skin, sclera, mucous membranes, and urine, apparently due to the color of the medication itself. Some constitutional effects such as nausea, headache, and injection site reactions have occurred, as well as a reduction in lymphocyte counts (which, however, remain within the normal range). Transient, self-limited elevations of systemic and diastolic blood pressure occurred in normal volunteers. Rarely, easily treated allergic reactions occurred in normal volunteers. However, in a retrospective French study of 739 patients admitted to one of 21 ICUs for smoke inhalation, 386 (55.2%) received hydroxocobalamin and those who received the drug had an increased risk of acute kidney injury (AKI) and severe AKI after adjusting for risk factors but no difference in survival. In addition, authors of a retrospective case series of 27 patients found a temporal association of administration of hydroxocobalamin with methemoglobinemia which occurred in 6 of 27 cases. However, in a retrospective cohort study of 36 patients with suspected inhalation injury treated with hydroxocobalamin and 32 matched control patients with inhalation injury who were not treated with hydroxocobalamin, there were no significant differences in initial, final, peak, or change in methemoglobin levels or in relevant outcomes between groups. Finally, hydroxocobalamin can interfere with analysis of chemistry and coagulation analytes.

Indication: hydroxocobalamin (Cyanokit) is indicated for known or suspected cyanide poisoning and, because of its favorable safety profile, is suitable for empirical administration to enclosed-space fire smoke inhalation victims, especially concomitant burn victims. In one review, indications of cyanide toxicity in smoke inhalation victims are: a history of an enclosed-space fire scene, oropharyngeal soot or carbonaceous expectorations, any alteration of consciousness, and inexplicable hypotension (systolic blood pressure ≤90 mm Hg in adults).

In a decision-analysis model, use of hydroxocobalamin in patients with known or suspected cyanide poisoning from closed-space fire smoke inhalation decreased per-patient hospital costs by $7226, largely due to decreased hospital length of stay.

In a retrospective case-control study of 138 smoke inhalation adult victims administered hydroxocobalamin (2008-2014) and 135 historical controls (2002-2008), mortality rates were similar at 29% and 28%. However, hydroxocobalamin administration was associated with a significantly lower pneumonia rate (23% vs. 49%) and fewer ventilator days (4 days vs. 7 days) compared to controls.

A carboxyhemoglobin level >30% was associated with a fatal outcome in the UK series (OR 7.0; 95% CI 1.5-33.7) and there was positive moderate correlation between carboxyhemoglobin and the Poisoning Severity Score (r = 0.57). The Poisoning Severity Score is determined based on a chart organized by body system that lists symptoms, signs and selected clinical chemistry and results in a score indicating minor, moderate or severe toxicity for each system.

The Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) is used to predict mortality in patients with sepsis. In a study including all patients (n=136) admitted for severe burns at the burn ICU of Tours University Hospital between 2017 and 2020 and who stayed 3 days or more, there was a significant association between DeltaSOFA, defined as day 3 SOFA minus day 0 SOFA, and mortality that persisted after adjustment for age and total body surface area burned (HR 1.37, 95 %CI 1.09-1.72). Area under the receiver operating characteristics curve for prediction of mortality by day 0 SOFA and deltaSOFA were 0.79 (95 %CI 0.69-0.89) and 0.83 (95 %CI 0.70-0.95), respectively.

Rare sequelae in survivors of severe acute poisoning have included delayed development of Parkinsonian-like states and encephalopathies with memory deficits and personality changes. Lesions in the globus pallidus and putamen may be noted on CT or MRI scans. In one case report of a 45-year-old Yemeni woman with cyanide poisoning due to smoke inhalation, after three months of treatment and continuous follow-up, she continued to have mild cognitive memory impairment along with word-finding difficulties and focal dystonia of her right hand.
Organ donation: cyanide-poisoned patients proved to be brain dead have been successful organ donors (liver, heart, lungs, corneas, kidneys).
